title: SE201 Lesson 7: Skills as building blocks

data.sub: From loop to enterprise systems  •  clarkhuang.github.io

scenes.text: Why would three capable agents do the same job three different ways? [pause] Take our made-up subscription-billing system. Now and then, someone asks for a new plan, or a new price. The first time, an agent works out the four steps, and gets it right. The second time, a different agent starts from zero, and skips the tax setup. The third time, another one edits the old price in place, and every existing subscriber is on the new price. [pause] Same job. Three results. Nobody wrote down how.

data.label: A MADE-UP EXAMPLE  ·  THE JOB: ADD A PLAN, OR A NEW PRICE, TO THE BILLING SYSTEM

scenes.text: Software keeps finding new units of reuse. Libraries: shared code. Frameworks: an application's structure. Services: something running, behind an A.P.I. [pause] All three reuse software. A skill reuses something different: <emphasis>how a job gets done.</emphasis> One recurring job, written down, tested, and shared.

data.label: UNITS OF REUSE  ·  ROUGHLY IN THE ORDER THEY BECAME COMMON
data.caption:
A skill reuses how a job gets done:
one recurring job, written down, tested, and shared.

scenes.text: Several agent tools now share a format for this: a folder, with an instruction file. It starts with when to use it: someone asks for a new plan, or a new price. That line is how an agent finds the skill. Then the inputs: name, price, billing period, start date. If one is missing, the agent asks. It doesn't guess.

scenes.text: If that sounds like a runbook, it is. Engineers have written those for decades. What's changed is the reader. A person reads a runbook now and then, and fills the gaps from memory. An agent reads the skill on every run, with no memory of the last. Where the page is silent, it guesses. [pause] And when a step needs no judgment, make it a script the skill calls.

data.label: IT’S A RUNBOOK  ·  WHAT’S CHANGED IS THE READER

bands.label: A RUNBOOK  ·  READ BY A PERSON
A SKILL  ·  READ BY AN AGENT

nodes.text: Read on every run, no memory of the last
Where the page is silent, it guesses
A step that needs no judgment?  Make it a script the skill calls.

scenes.text: So treat a skill like code. Keep it in the repository, versioned, and reviewed when it changes. [pause] And test it. Hand it to a fresh agent that has never seen the job, and let it run on staging. If it can't finish from the page alone, the skill isn't done.

data.label: TEST IT WITH A FRESH AGENT

nodes.text: Can’t finish from the page alone?  The skill isn’t done.

data.caption: Treat a skill like code: in the repo, versioned, reviewed.

scenes.text: Now run those three jobs again, from the skill. Same steps. Same checks. [pause] No guarantee: agents still vary. That's what the checks are for. And when a run goes wrong, don't just fix the run. Fix the skill. One change, in one place, and every later run gets it. That's a building block: reliable enough to build on.

data.label: THE SAME THREE RUNS  ·  THIS TIME FROM THE SKILL
data.caption: When a run goes wrong, fix the skill, not just the run.

scenes.text: So when is a job worth a skill? The first time? The third? Or never, because agents can work it out? [pause] A good rule of thumb: <emphasis>the third time.</emphasis> Once, you're learning. Twice, you see the pattern. The third time, write it down. Sooner, if a mistake costs money.

data.label: A RULE OF THUMB

scenes.text: So, to recap. One recurring job, written down, with its checks and its traps. In the repo, tested by a fresh agent. And when a run goes wrong, fix the skill.

scenes.text: Which gives us rule seven, for your agents. When a job comes back a third time, write it as a skill: when to use it, inputs, steps, checks, and traps. Keep it in the repo, and test it with a fresh agent. And when a run goes wrong, fix the skill, not just the run.

scenes.text: Now, your turn. Pick a job you've explained to your A.I. more than twice. Ask it to draft the skill. [pause] Then open a fresh chat, give it only that page, and see if the job gets done.

scenes.text: One skill does one job. But real work is a chain of jobs, and some of it should start on its own. That's next: routines, pipelines, and integration. See you in lesson eight.
